keyVerseText: Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying,
rootMeaning: The Greek adjective ὅλος (hólos) is a primary word with no known root derivation, signifying completeness or entirety. Its core sense conveys something that is whole, entire, or complete in all its parts, whether in extent, amount, or time. This nuance goes beyond the simple English gloss of "whole" or "all" by emphasizing an undivided, thorough completeness, often used to describe something as intact and unified.
usageInScripture: With 112 total occurrences, ὅλος is frequently translated as "all" (61 times) and "the whole" (28 times), showing its consistent use to denote totality or completeness. It appears in various grammatical constructions, sometimes preceding or following nouns, and can function substantively, highlighting its flexibility in expressing the fullness or entirety of persons, things, or concepts. This range in translation reveals the word's broad application in Scripture to emphasize comprehensive inclusion or entirety.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ὅλος enriches our grasp of biblical teaching on God's creation, providence, and redemption as complete and perfect. The word underscores God's sovereign work as not partial but whole and entire, reflecting His holiness and the fullness of salvation offered in Christ. It reminds believers that God's promises and actions are thorough and all-encompassing, inviting faith in His perfect and unbroken provision. This completeness also challenges Christians to live fully surrendered to God, reflecting the wholeness of their new identity in Christ.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 1:22, the phrase "Now all this was done" uses ὅλος to emphasize the entirety of the events leading to the fulfillment of prophecy. The word highlights that nothing was omitted or partial in God's plan; everything happened fully as spoken by the Lord through the prophet. This stresses the certainty and completeness of God's promises being realized in Christ's birth, encouraging trust in the divine orchestration of salvation history.
